items.title: A Scoping Review on Intelligent Computing upon Silicon Photonics and Optical Network on Chips
items.abstract: The continuous expansion of data-intensive applications, including deep learning, autonomous control, and real-time analytics, has pushed conventional electronic computing toward its limits in performance and energy efficiency. Combining silicon photonics with Optical Network on Chip (ONoC) provides a pathway toward high-bandwidth and low-latency communication with reduced power consumption, positioning these technologies as promising enablers for next-generation intelligent systems. This work systematically reviews current efforts to integrate silicon photonics and ONoC architectures with Artificial Intelligence (AI) models such as Machine Learning (ML), Deep Neural Network (DNN), and Large Language Model (LLM), highlighting recent progress, application areas, and open research challenges. A structured literature review was carried out across two focus areas, each searched and screened as a separate stream: (1) Optical Neural Network (ONN) developed for AI inference and training, and (2) ML-based optimization techniques applied to ONoC design. Peer-reviewed studies, and preprints under an explicitly stated rule, were examined with attention to device-level innovations, architectural co-design, acceleration of AI workloads, and photonic-aware system optimization. Recent studies report advances in photonic devices such as modulators, detectors, and microring resonators, along with hybrid photonic–electronic architectures and AI-optimized routing frameworks. ONN implementations demonstrate high-speed, low-energy computation, while ML-assisted methods have improved ONoC performance in wavelength allocation, fault tolerance, and security. Despite rapid progress, several technical challenges remain, including fabrication tolerances, thermal sensitivity, and the limited maturity of nonlinear photonic components. Current demonstrations are mainly at the prototype level, with few large-scale deployments, and because most studies are simulation-based, their reported performance figures should be regarded as upper bounds that still require verification on fabricated hardware. The convergence of silicon photonics, ONoCs, and AI computing represents a shift from purely electronic processing toward hybrid photonic–electronic platforms capable of supporting massive workloads efficiently. Future research should emphasize scalable fabrication processes, integrated photonic–electronic co-design, robust thermal management, and standardized frameworks to accelerate the adoption of these technologies in AI accelerators, data centers, and edge devices.

items.title: A Study on AI-Based Customer Relationship Management in Modern Commerce
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing how firms interpret customer records, support service employees and communicate across commercial channels. Its value depends on the quality of the relationship it helps maintain. This paper examines AI-based customer relationship management through a critical narrative review and descriptive analysis of published evidence. Nine journal articles are considered alongside official enterprise statistics and an AI risk framework. The review distinguishes ordinary CRM adoption from the deployment of AI within CRM. It also separates operational productivity from customer trust and durable commercial value. Two charts reproduce attributed Eurostat observations, while an original conceptual diagram connects data readiness, bounded assistance, human decisions and relationship outcomes. The synthesis suggests that useful deployment requires clear task boundaries, reliable knowledge sources, accessible correction and evaluation beyond response speed. A proposed implementation roadmap and research propositions identify ways to examine these conditions in future field studies. No primary survey, customer experiment or statistical hypothesis test is reported. The paper contributes a practical basis for studying AI-assisted relationships without treating software ownership, automation volume or conversational fluency as proof of customer benefit..

items.title: A System Dynamics Approach to AI Risk Governance and Organizational Resilience in SMEs: Modeling the Trade-off Between Innovation and Compliance
items.abstract: This paper is building a system dynamics model to investigate how the small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) can regulate artificial intelligence (AI) risk without reducing the innovation value that can be justified when implementing AI. The work contends that the relationship between innovation and compliance is not a linear kind of trade-off, but a dynamical regulatory system with feedback mechanisms whereby experimentation, deployment levels, risk exposure, governance mechanisms, learning routines, and resilience resources interact with one another through time. The paper incorporates the constructs of SMEs into a stock-flow simulation based on the dynamic capabilities theory, organizational resilience research, technology-organization-environment logic, AI risk management standards, and system dynamics. Findings indicate that innovation-first strategy generates rapid initial ability development and generates shadow AI, risks that were not fully resolved, more recovery time, and shorter resilience. Compliance first approach minimizes risk exposure at the cost of experimentation and introduces approval lag. Balanced adaptive governance is the strongest in the long-term outcome where tiered controls, learning loops, human oversight, and reusable compliance routines minimize risk without impacting the innovation throughput. The article adds a dynamic conceptualization of AI risk governance among SMEs and the leverage points to use by managers and policymakers aiming at responsible adoption of AI given the limited resources.

items.title: Accuracy and Safety of Three Large Language Models Answering Turkish Questions on Adult Immunization
items.abstract: Vaccine misinformation contributes to falling immunization coverage, and people increasingly bring vaccine questions to chatbots. We evaluated three large language models on 72 Turkish questions on adult immunization, in two arms: 40 patient-focused questions and 32 mapped to CDC/ACIP, WHO or Turkish Ministry of Health recommendations. The 216 responses were blind-coded and scored independently by two blinded specialists against a guideline-anchored answer key. Binary accuracy was 95.1% for Claude Opus 4.8, 93.8% for Gemini-3.1-Pro, and 86.1% for GPT-5.5. Patient-facing questions, including the classic vaccine myths, were answered well (93.8–96.2%), but accuracy on technical guideline content fell to 76.6% for GPT-5.5, which was also the most readable model and referred the reader to a clinician in only 53.1% of guideline-arm responses. Responses were more often incomplete than wrong.

items.title: Adaptive Digital Consciousness: An Evolutionary Framework for Human Identity Preservation Using Large Language Models
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) have greatly changed the interaction between man and machines through natural-language reasoning, content generation, personalization, and interaction via agents. However, traditional LLM applications do not provide a unified mechanism for maintaining a long-term, structured, and identity-consistent representation of a person during long-time interaction. As shown in the recent studies of generative agents, long-term LLM memory, agentic memory, lifelong learning, and AI self-identity, these processes present essential capabilities that have been studied as separate components. This paper presents the Adaptive Digital Consciousness (ADC) framework as the theoretical architecture for computational representation of core features of human identity. The ADC framework proposes a system of structured representation of Digital DNA for personal knowledge, experience, preferences, values, and behaviors and connects it to multilayer memory, semantic embeddings, vector retrieval, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), LLM reasoning, adaptive learning, and autonomous agents. The framework also proposes the notion of identity constraints and the system of updating memory, consolidating it, handling conflicts, forgetting, maintaining privacy, consent, and security, as well as monitoring the origin of digital information. The goal of the study is not to replicate biological or subjective consciousness The research motivation, previous works, the system suggested, as well as memory and adaptation techniques, evaluation techniques, ethics and applications of the findings, drawbacks of the research and future research directions on this subject.

items.title: Addressing Cyberbullying in Vietnam Through Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Cyberbullying is not only a growing concern for society as a whole, but especially for the education sector, as it disproportionately affects the youngest cohorts, undermining learning and psychological well-being. At the same time, the increasing accessibility of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), has begun to reshape how people communicate online. Against this background, this chapter examines cyberbullying in Vietnam through the lens of GenAI, highlighting both the negative and positive dimensions of this technological shift. Using an integrative review that combines international and local scholarship, the chapter summarizes the scope (including common types) and the psychosocial consequences of cyberbullying in Vietnam. The review draws on peer-reviewed studies and local reports, organizing the findings into thematic domains to form a pragmatic analytic framework for practice and policy. The chapter then considers how GenAI capabilities – automated content generation, personalization, and deepfake technologies – may increase the speed, reach, and ambiguity of harassment, making harmful behaviors harder to identify and respond to. Conversely, it discusses the potential of AI-enabled tools for detection, moderation, risk assessment, and early warning to strengthen community- and school-based prevention systems that can be integrated with GenAI. The chapter also addresses fundamental technical and governance issues, including algorithmic bias, transparency and explainability, privacy and data protection, and safeguards for child rights in digital contexts. Overall, it argues that GenAI-based responses are likely to be effective only when integrated with Vietnamese language use, culturally specific communication norms, and existing institutional capacities. By situating Vietnam within global conversations on cyberbullying and GenAI, the chapter offers contextually appropriate recommendations to support responsible, ethical, and protective uses of GenAI for safer online spaces.

items.title: Advanced Backend Technologies using MongoDB: A Scalable NoSQL Database for Modern Web, Cloud, and AI Applications
items.abstract: Modern web applications require databases that provide high performance, flexibility, and scalability to manage large volumes of structured and unstructured data. Traditional relational databases often face challenges in handling rapidly changing application requirements. MongoDB, a leading NoSQL document-oriented database, addresses these challenges through its flexible schema, distributed architecture, and cloud-native capabilities. This paper presents a study of MongoDB and its role in advanced backend technologies. It discusses MongoDB's document model, replication, sharding, indexing, and aggregation framework along with its integration with modern backend frameworks such as Node.js, Express.js, FastAPI, and Spring Boot. The paper also explores MongoDB Atlas for cloud deployment and its applications in microservices, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Internet of Things (IoT), and Big Data. A comparison with traditional SQL databases is provided to evaluate performance, scalability, and flexibility. The study concludes that MongoDB is an efficient and future-ready database solution for building secure, scalable, and high-performance backend applications.

items.title: Advanced Ventilation Systems in Interior Spaces: Improving Indoor Air Quality and Human Comfort
items.abstract: Indoor environments have become a critical area of research due to the increasing amount of time people spend inside buildings and the growing recognition of the relationship between indoor environmental quality and human health. Modern buildings are increasingly designed with improved insulation and airtight construction to enhance energy efficiency; however, these strategies can unintentionally reduce natural air exchange and contribute to the accumulation of indoor pollutants. Poor indoor air quality (IAQ), caused by elevated carbon dioxide (CO₂), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), biological contaminants, and excessive humidity, can negatively affect occupant health, comfort, cognitive performance, and productivity. Advanced ventilation systems have emerged as an essential solution for maintaining healthy indoor environments while achieving energy efficiency goals. Unlike conventional ventilation approaches that provide fixed airflow rates, advanced systems incorporate adaptive technologies such as demand-controlled ventilation, heat and energy recovery ventilation, displacement ventilation, personalized ventilation, and intelligent ventilation systems supported by Internet of Things (IoT) sensors and artificial intelligence (AI). These systems continuously monitor indoor conditions and adjust ventilation performance according to occupancy levels, pollutant concentrations, and environmental parameters. This review paper examines the development, operational principles, and applications of advanced ventilation technologies in interior spaces. It explores their role in improving indoor air quality, enhancing thermal comfort, reducing energy consumption, and supporting sustainable interior design practices. The paper also discusses the integration of smart monitoring systems, occupant-centered ventilation strategies, and future directions toward adaptive and self-learning building environments. Through a comprehensive analysis of existing research, this review highlights the importance of advanced ventilation systems as a fundamental component of healthy, efficient, and human-centered interior spaces.

items.title: Advancing neurosurgical practice with augmented reality: a single-center real-world case series with illustrated technical notes
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE The aim of this study was to evaluate the real-world application and clinical value of a head-mounted augmented reality (AR) navigation platform across a wide range of neurosurgical pathologies and procedures. METHODS In this real-world retrospective case series, the authors assessed 105 neurosurgical procedures performed by 8 neurosurgeons at a single center from January 2024 to March 2026. A head-mounted AR navigation platform (SurgicalAR, Cranial Navigation, and Spine Navigation; Medivis) was used in all procedures. Video records were available for all cases. Clinical and pathological data, surgical approaches, types of reference frames, and registration methods were systematically collected. The workflow for each surgical approach was characterized in detail. RESULTS This analysis included 105 cases (60 female, mean age 53.5). Cranial surgeries (n = 92, 87.6%) were most common, predominantly for tumors (n = 69, 65.7%), with meningioma (22.9%) and glioblastoma (19.0%) as the leading pathologies. Custom reference frames (n = 57) and surface registration (n = 93) were the most frequently used techniques in cranial navigation. In cranial tumor surgery, gross-total resection was achieved in 62 of 69 cases, supported by multimodal AR planning. In spine surgery, all 34 pedicle screws placed with the Spine Navigation system achieved a Gertzbein-Robbins grade of A. AR was also successfully applied to cerebrovascular, puncture-based, and functional surgery. CONCLUSIONS Head-mounted AR navigation was feasible across diverse procedures, but its value depended on case selection, registration reliability, and workflow. It was most useful for multimodal tumor planning, pedicle screw placement, and percutaneous interventions; conventional navigation or direct anatomical guidance remained necessary when AR accuracy or ergonomics were inadequate. These findings support AR as a significant advancement in future neurosurgical practice.

items.title: Advancing value creation in B2B market research – a human–AI collaboration framework for large language model
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how prompt design influences the quality of large language model (LLM)-generated business-to-business (B2B) market research outputs. It also proposes a switch-point governance mechanism for converting LLM-generated drafts into decision-ready market intelligence artefacts. Design/methodology/approach The study uses an exploratory pilot evaluation of three market-facing LLM-based tools: ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity AI. The tools are compared across three benchmark B2B market research tasks and three prompt types: basic, context-augmented and role-specific. In total, 81 outputs were generated. A role-specific benchmark subset of 27 outputs was then assessed using automated metrics and blinded human ratings. The automated metrics included relevance through cosine similarity, reference overlap through ROUGE-F1, cross-run semantic stability, latency, token length and readability through Flesch Reading Ease. Human evaluators rated the outputs on relevance, completeness, factuality, instruction-following and insightfulness. One-way ANOVA and non-parametric checks are reported as exploratory task-level tests, not as confirmatory evidence of model superiority. Findings Role-specific prompts produced the strongest descriptive scores in this pilot setting. Within the benchmark subset, Gemini showed the strongest observed profile, with higher average relevance, reference overlap and semantic stability, along with lower latency. ChatGPT produced relevant outputs but tended to generate longer and less readable drafts. Perplexity generated concise and readable summaries, but its outputs were less aligned with the reference brief and decision-facing requirements. Human ratings followed a similar descriptive pattern. Cross-run semantic stability showed directional alignment with higher decision-readiness ratings, offering preliminary support for P1. The proposed switch-point matrix illustrates P2 by mapping automated confidence signals and human judgement to four escalation actions: accept, judge, review/redo and rewrite. Research limitations/implications The study is an exploratory pilot case. The task set is small, and the task-level ANOVA is based on only three observations per tool. The findings may also vary across domains, model versions, prompt libraries and organisational contexts. Future research should expand the task bank, include more B2B sectors, use larger rater pools, compare additional model versions and test the switch-point thresholds in live market intelligence workflows. Practical implications The study provides a replicable workflow for B2B market intelligence teams. It shows how teams can standardise prompt design, screen LLM-generated outputs, combine automated checks with human evaluation and allocate decision rights through transparent escalation rules. Social implications The framework supports accountable use of LLM-based market research by reducing the risk that persuasive but weakly grounded claims enter managerial decision-making. It also highlights the need for human oversight; evidence checks and traceable governance in AI-supported knowledge work. Originality/value The study extends service-dominant logic to LLM-mediated B2B market research by treating LLM outputs as candidate value propositions rather than finished knowledge products. Its main contribution is the operationalisation of decision-rights governance through cross-run semantic stability and switch-point logic.

items.title: Aesthetics in form and Function: Ergonomic Analysis of Juice Glassware
items.abstract: Glassware serves both functional and experiential roles in juice service, where design influences usability, visual appeal, and perceived capacity. This study examines the ergonomic and aesthetic attributes of commonly used glassware and their effects on volumetric efficiency and user experience. Glass samples collected from juice shops across the Vellore district, Tamil Nadu, were analysed through empirical observation. Ergonomic parameters included grip comfort, stability, dimensional balance, and weight distribution, while aesthetic qualities such as form, clarity, texture, and design language were evaluated through structured user surveys. Findings indicate that Collins glasses are the predominant choice for fresh juice, with mason jars and standard bottles also preferred, whereas sling and pint glasses are seldom selected. Overall, 84% of users favoured ergonomically optimised designs. The study concludes that combining ergonomic efficiency with aesthetic coherence enhances functionality, presentation, and consumer satisfaction.

items.title: AI adoption statistics 2026: How far along is your industry?
items.abstract: AI adoption is moving quickly, but not every company or industry is progressing at the same pace. Some organizations have already integrated AI into daily operations, while others are still experimenting with early use cases. Looking at AI adoption statistics can help business leaders understand where the market stands and whether their own company is ahead, catching up, or still at the beginning of the adoption journey. What AI adoption statistics reveal AI adoption data provides more than a snapshot of how many companies are using artificial intelligence. It can also show how businesses move from experimentation to practical implementation and where AI is becoming part of everyday operations. For companies planning their next steps, AI adoption statistics can provide useful context. They help decision makers compare their progress with broader market activity and understand whether investment in AI is accelerating across their sector. AI adoption by industry Different sectors face different challenges when adopting AI. AI adoption by industry can vary depending on available data, regulatory requirements, technical maturity, business processes, and the types of problems companies are trying to solve. Healthcare, finance, retail, manufacturing, and professional services may all approach AI differently. Some industries can introduce automation and analytics quickly, while others need more preparation before AI can be integrated into critical workflows. Understanding these differences helps companies compare themselves with organizations operating in similar environments rather than treating AI adoption as a single market-wide trend. Enterprise AI adoption For large organizations, AI adoption often becomes more complicated once companies move beyond individual pilots. Enterprise AI adoption statistics can show how businesses are scaling AI across departments, where investments are being made, and which obstacles continue to slow broader implementation. Common challenges may include data readiness, internal skills, coordination between teams, and the ability to connect AI initiatives with clear business goals. Looking at enterprise adoption patterns can help decision makers understand what other organizations are prioritizing and where implementation often becomes difficult. AI adoption trends in 2026 Current AI adoption trends suggest that companies are increasingly focused on practical results rather than experimentation alone. Businesses are looking at how AI can improve operations, customer experience, analytics, and automation while delivering measurable value. However, adoption still depends heavily on factors such as industry maturity, data quality, internal expertise, and leadership support. Companies that understand these constraints can set more realistic expectations and prioritize AI initiatives that are more likely to succeed. Final thoughts AI adoption in 2026 is not happening at the same speed everywhere. Some businesses are already scaling AI across operations, while others are still building the foundations needed for successful implementation. By examining AI adoption statistics, AI adoption by industry, enterprise AI adoption statistics, and broader AI adoption trends, companies can better understand their position in the market and make more informed decisions about where to focus their next AI investments.

items.title: AI and Machine Learning for API Security
items.abstract: This research paper explores the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) in enhancing Application Programming Interface (API) security. It focuses on real-time API monitoring, anomaly detection, behavioral analysis, threat identification, risk classification, and automated security responses. The study reviews six existing research works and proposes an AI-driven security framework that classifies incoming API requests into three categories: safe, suspicious, and malicious. Based on the identified risk level, the proposed system aims to allow legitimate requests, verify suspicious activities, and block potentially harmful requests while maintaining security logs for further analysis. The paper also highlights key challenges, including false alarms, data quality, computational requirements, and adapting to evolving cyber threats. It presents a conceptual framework and future evaluation approach to support the development of more intelligent, adaptive, and reliable API security systems.

items.title: AI and the Right to Privacy: A Comparative Study of India and the European Union
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has turned privacy from a question of disclosure alone into one of continuous data collection, inference, prediction and consequential decision-making. This Article asks whether Indian law offers protection against such forms of data-intensive power that is as layered as that of the European Union. It adopts a doctrinal and comparative approach, analysing constitutional rights, data protection laws, artificial intelligence legislation, key case law, institutional documents and enforcement data. India has a solid constitutional framework for dignity, autonomy and proportionality, but its statutory framework is less specific on solely automated decisions, explanations, meaningful human intervention, biometric surveillance and model training. This gap is widened by the phased commencement of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, under which a number of substantive obligations had yet to come into force as of September 2026. The European Union, by comparison, combines the Charter of Fundamental Rights, the General Data Protection Regulation and the Artificial Intelligence Act, producing more detailed rules on lawful processing, sensitive data, automated decisions, risk management and transparency. The European model is nonetheless fragmented and highly technical, especially on model training, data inferred by models, and the blurred boundary between data protection law and the new artificial intelligence law. The comparison points to a calibrated Indian reform agenda built on contestability, high-risk impact assessment, biometric safeguards, training-data accountability and independent technical oversight, rather than wholesale transplantation of the European Union regime.

items.title: AI Anxiety, Familiarity and Privacy Concerns: The Mediating Role of AI Literacy and the Moderating Role of Technophobia
items.abstract: This study examines how AI anxiety and familiarity relate to privacy concerns through AI literacy, and whether technophobia moderates the literacy–privacy relationship. Using survey data from 3,000 generative AI users in China and partial least squares structural equation modeling, we find that both familiarity and, contrary to expectations, anxiety are positively associated with AI literacy. AI literacy, in turn, is associated with greater privacy concerns and mediates both relationships, suggesting that increased knowledge may heighten awareness of data risks. Technophobia weakens the positive association between AI literacy and privacy concerns, although more technophobic users report higher overall concern. Exploratory age-group analyses suggest that the positive anxiety–literacy association is especially apparent among users in their 40s. These findings reveal a privacy awareness paradox and highlight the value of AI education that combines technical understanding, privacy awareness, and attention to users’ emotional responses.

items.title: AI Enhanced Anomaly Detection of System Logs in Cybersecurity
items.abstract: System logs contain valuable information about authentication attempts, application events, operating system activities, and potential cybersecurity threats. However, manually analysing large volumes of log data is time-consuming and may delay the detection of suspicious activities. This paper presents an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enhanced system for detecting anomalous patterns in system logs using machine learning techniques. The proposed workflow includes log collection, preprocessing, time-window aggregation, feature extraction, anomaly scoring, threshold-based classification, and security alert generation. Isolation Forest is used as the primary unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm and is compared with Local Outlier Factor (LOF), One-Class Support Vector Machine (SVM), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) autoencoder. The evaluation uses a simulated dataset containing 30,000 one-hour activity windows, including 1,050 injected anomaly windows. The reported results show that Isolation Forest achieves a precision of 0.594, recall of 0.553, F1-score of 0.573, ROC-AUC of 0.962, and average precision of 0.613. Although Isolation Forest provides a lightweight detection approach, the comparison indicates that other methods achieve higher F1-scores under the reported experimental conditions. The findings highlight the importance of threshold selection, class imbalance, and multiple evaluation metrics in anomaly detection. The proposed workflow provides a foundation for cybersecurity monitoring and suspicious-activity prioritisation. Further validation using real-world enterprise logs is required to establish its effectiveness in practical deployment.

items.title: AI Facilitation of Online Disagreement
items.abstract: AI has considerable potential to facilitate online discussions and reduce conflict, but designers of such systems face the risk of algorithmic aversion. Past studies have found that people judge identical messages less favorably when they believe they were written by AI. However, as AI becomes more integrated into everyday life and people gain experience with AI facilitators, this aversion may diminish. It also remains unclear how much the content of a facilitator's message matters relative to its human or AI label, and whether the facilitation strategies people prefer actually improve the conversation. Finally, because most people observe rather than participate in online discussions, it is important to understand whether AI facilitators are perceived differently by observers and participants. To address these questions, we conducted two complementary studies examining perceptions of different facilitation strategies and their effects on actual conversations. In a vignette experiment (N = 388), we crossed the facilitator's label (AI or human) with ten facilitation strategies. In a live conversation experiment, an LLM used five of these strategies to facilitate 20-minute text chats between 188 pairs of people who disagreed on political and non-political topics. Participants preferred the kind of facilitator they had experienced. After seeing an AI facilitator, 30% wanted one in future discussions, against 7% after seeing a human facilitator. The AI label lowered ratings of the facilitator's warmth and competence, but the strategy mattered far more, explaining 11% of the variance in ratings against less than 1% explained by the label. Participants preferred facilitators that showed understanding over facilitators that reminded them of community norms. However, the strategies people preferred did not reliably change the conversations. Observers and participants in live conversations ranked the strategies similarly. In summary, the AI vs. human label matters far less than what the facilitator actually says. A well-designed process can improve user perceptions more than enough to offset algorithmic aversion.

items.title: AI in Indian Healthcare: Promise, Pitfalls, and the Path Forward
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping healthcare in India through diagnostic imaging, predictive analytics, robotic surgery, patient monitoring, and hospital workflow automation. These innovations promise improved diagnostic accuracy, operational efficiency, and expanded access to care, particularly in resource-limited settings. Yet, accelerated adoption raises critical challenges, including inadequate regulation, weak data governance, cybersecurity risks, patient privacy concerns, and algorithmic bias, which may undermine trust and equitable care delivery. This study employed a mixed-methods design to explore perceptions of 69 purposively sampled healthcare professionals across India. A structured questionnaire assessed familiarity with AI, perceived benefits, skill-related challenges, ethical concerns, and regulatory awareness. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, while qualitative responses underwent Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis. Extracted themes were further subjected to Pareto analysis and a policy priority matrix to identify the most pressing issues. Findings show that 75.3% of participants were familiar with AI, with many recognizing its role in improving work quality (68.1%), efficiency (68.1%), and supporting clinical judgment (65.2%). However, 59% feared reduced cognitive engagement. Most (86.9%) emphasized the urgent need for new skill sets. Thematic analysis identified key concerns included limited regulatory awareness (n39), training and continuous learning needs (n25), data privacy and security (n15), patient care benefits (n13), risks of breaches and unauthorized access (n12) and specific guideline or bills(n12). The study highlights the need for comprehensive training, robust ethical and regulatory frameworks, and strong data governance to balance AI's benefits with its risks in Indian healthcare.

items.title: AI in Long-Term Care: A Closed-Loop Sociotechnical Reliability Framework
items.abstract: AI is increasingly used in long-term care (LTC), yet reliability is often judged at the level of individual models or devices. This is insufficient in LTC, where residents vary in capacity, autonomy, and preferences. Their ability to question AI outputs may fluctuate, and care delivery depends on distributed roles and finite operational capacity. We define sociotechnical reliability as the capacity of an AI-enabled care system to consistently translate resident-relevant information into appropriate and timely care actions under real-world LTC conditions, with failures that are detectable and correctable across the care pathway. In this Viewpoint, we draw on professional experience overseeing AI initiatives across LTC and hospital settings, examined in relation to a purposively mapped interdisciplinary literature, to inform the development of a reliability framework. Our aim is to reframe AI reliability in LTC as an end-to-end care system property and to provide a framework for identifying where reliability is gained, lost, and evaluated. We propose 5 reliability functions: sensing, inference, verification and contextualization, response and escalation, and learning and adaptation, with governance and accountability operating across all 5 functions. The framework highlights recurrent failures, including incomplete sensing, nonportable inference, overreliance on or dismissal of AI outputs during verification, unclear ownership or delayed response, and repeated failures without correction. The framework also makes reliability empirically examinable through questions about where the pathway fails, who has the authority to verify and act, whether response demands are sustainable within available capacity, and whether failures become visible to governance and inform learning and adaptation. Our central viewpoint is that AI in LTC should be judged not by model performance alone but by whether the surrounding care system can reliably translate AI-generated information into care.

items.title: AI in tourism and hospitality: from predictive infrastructure to experiential interface
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to review the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) research in tourism and hospitality (T&H), tracing its shift from back-end analytical infrastructure to front-stage experiential interface. This study maps conceptual foundations, thematic dynamics and methodological patterns, with particular attention to generative AI (GenAI), and develops a future research agenda for responsible and sustainability-oriented AI innovation. Design/methodology/approach This study conducted a longitudinal bibliometric and thematic review of 1, 851 peer-reviewed articles (1986–2025) from Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection. Following the PRISMA guidelines, VOSviewer and Gephi were used for co-occurrence and citation mapping, interpreting thematic evolution across four historical phases to inform a theory-driven research agenda. Findings Two trajectories structure the field: AI as analytical infrastructure (optimizing forecasting and decision-making) and AI as experiential interface (facilitating generative, interactive and emotionally embedded service encounters). The field has evolved from symbolic logic and data mining to multimodal analytics, service robots and GenAI applications. The proposed agenda highlights methodological transparency, ethical and accountable AI, human–AI collaboration, employee welfare and sustainable transformation. Originality/value This study offers a structured, theory-informed synthesis of AI research in T&H. By linking historical trajectories with emerging priorities, it helps scholars, practitioners and policymakers understand where AI creates value, where risks arise and how future T&H research can respond to the GenAI era.

items.title: AI Innovative Practical Teaching Model for Interdisciplinary Postgraduates Integrated with OBE Concept
items.abstract: Traditional postgraduate education faces challenges in personalized guidance, dynamic competency tracking, and interdisciplinary practical training. This study proposed an AI-driven practical teaching model for interdisciplinary postgraduates based on the Outcomes-Based Education (OBE) concept. We adopted AI-assisted English learning as a representative application scenario and constructed a closed-loop teaching framework that integrates multi-agent collaboration, Large Language Models (LLM), and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The framework establishes a multidimensional learner state model and a learning benefit function to support dynamic learner modeling, personalized task allocation, and intelligent feedback. We conducted a ten-week classroom teaching experiment involving interdisciplinary postgraduate students. The experiment compared three modes: traditional instruction, AI-agent-supported learning, and the integrated RAG–LLM teaching framework. The experimental results show that the proposed framework improves learning-path stability, and promote balanced development of vocabulary, grammar, listening, and speaking abilities. It also enhances the effectiveness and interpretability of feedback. The integrated RAG–LLM architecture facilitates the transition from passive learning to active learning. It also strengthens learner autonomy and strategic decision-making. This study provides an OBE-oriented AI teaching framework that integrate multi-agent collaboration with LLM and RAG technologies. The framework offers practical guidance for intelligent education and interdisciplinary postgraduate training.

items.title: AI literacy and vocational students’ complex problem-solving skills: a moderated mediation model of systematic thinking, cognitive load, and perceived school ICT support
items.abstract: As technological advancements such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) reshape the landscape of work, career development in vocational education is increasingly oriented toward dynamic, long-term personal growth. In this context, Complex Problem-Solving Skills (CPS) have become a critical competence, reflecting students’ capacity to address ill-structured tasks and adapt to rapidly changing environments. Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines the relationship between AI Literacy and students’ self-reported Complex Problem-Solving Skills (CPS) in higher vocational colleges and the cognitive pathways that may help explain this relationship. This study posits that AI Literacy, as a personal agentic factor, is positively associated with self-reported CPS both directly and indirectly through Systematic Thinking Skills and cognitive load, and that perceived school information and communication technology (ICT) support may condition the strength of these associations. To provide temporal separation among the focal measures, a multi-wave survey was administered to 784 students from six higher vocational institutions at three time points. Data were analyzed using SPSS and Mplus. Results indicated that AI Literacy was significantly associated with self-reported CPS, with significant indirect effects estimated through Systematic Thinking Skills and the six-item cognitive-load composite. Notably, the associations between AI Literacy and these cognitive factors were stronger at higher levels of perceived school ICT support. These findings highlight the relevance of AI Literacy and students’ perceptions of ICT support to self-reported CPS and their preparation for AI-integrated workplaces.

items.title: AI Provenance and the Evaluation of Intellectual Work: Rational Risk, Social Meaning, and Human–AI Performance
items.abstract: AI can improve a piece of intellectual work while knowledge of its use can reduce the credit or trust that the work receives. Understanding that possibility requires separating what AI did to performance from what disclosure adds to evaluation. We connect these questions by asking what the evaluator intends to assess. Improvement relative to a producer’s unaided baseline may matter when the objective is better output; a different benchmark is needed when the objective is to measure unaided capability, assign intellectual credit, or allocate opportunities. A binary “AI was used” label supplies little information about those distinctions. Its relevance depends on the function AI performed, the authority the human retained, verification, and the object of evaluation. Negative reactions may reflect expected error or checking cost, an institutional requirement, social meanings concerning effort and authenticity, or a combination of these explanations. We examine how evidence can distinguish them without treating every penalty as stigma. We then follow evaluation back into production: anticipated disclosure can change whether and how people use AI, including whether they forgo useful assistance. As technology and institutions evolve, the practical question remains whether provenance-based treatment serves the evaluation’s stated purpose or substitutes a category judgment for more direct evidence.

items.title: AI-Assisted Imaging for Suspected Adolescent Endometriosis: Perspectives from Qualitative Focus Groups
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted imaging may support recognition of endometriosis, but perspectives on its use in adolescent care remain unclear. This study explored young people, parents, and health professionals’ views on its potential benefits, acceptable roles, perceived risks, and safeguards. Methods: Four semi-structured focus groups were conducted with adolescents aged 14–17 years (n = 3), young adults aged 18–25 years (n = 9), parents or carers (n = 5), and health professionals (n = 13). Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Four themes were developed: (1) diagnostic support, (2) human–AI collaboration, (3) automation bias and diagnostic harm, and (4) responsible AI use. Participants were cautiously hopeful that AI could improve image quality, identify subtle or missed findings, and reduce interpretive variation, but supported it only as an adjunct to skilled clinical care. They feared that apparently objective negative outputs could create false reassurance, reinforce diagnostic dismissal, and restrict further investigation. Trust depended on adolescent-relevant validation, representative data, transparent communication and consent, clear accountability, and clinicians retaining the expertise and authority to question or override AI outputs. Conclusion: AI-assisted imaging should strengthen rather than replace clinical judgment, and a negative AI-assisted imaging result should not prevent further assessment when symptoms persist.

items.title: AI-associated linguistic shifts in Swedish university theses: a corpus-level analysis, 2020–2025
items.abstract: Surveys document widespread student use of generative AI, yet corpus-level evidence of how post-ChatGPT thesis writing has changed remains scarce. We analysed approximately 17,000 Swedish bachelor's and master's theses from six universities, spanning the release of ChatGPT (2020–2025), scoring each on five language dimensions with OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini and grouping them into six topical clusters. Across the corpus, four writing-quality dimensions — grammar, vocabulary, academic quality, and wordiness — rose together after 2022, a modest but statistically clear change of trend that coincides with the release rather than continuing any earlier drift. The shift was present in every discipline, including fields that the published-research literature does not flag, and its disciplinary ordering was inverted relative to that literature: theses in Sustainability and Society changed most, those in Informatics and Engineering least. The rater's own AI-likelihood judgment, by contrast, proved unreliable — it rated more polished writing as less likely to be AI-generated, the opposite of what AI-text detection assumes, and was structurally miscalibrated against its own language-quality scores. Taken together, the results point to a linguistic shift consistent with AI-influenced writing across Swedish thesis prose, while cautioning that the direct AI-likelihood signal cannot be trusted and that analyses of this kind should rest on the language-quality dimensions instead.

items.title: AI-Based Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Accurate Brain Tumor Classification from MRI Images Using CNN and Vision Transformer
items.abstract: Brain tumors remain among the most life-threatening neurological disorders, and their outcome depends heavily on how early and how accurately they are diagnosed. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the modality of choice for tumor evaluation, yet manual reading of MRI scans is slow and subject to inter-observer disagreement. This paper proposes NeuroFusionNet, a lightweight hybrid deep learning framework that fuses a MobileNetV2-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) branch with a Vision Transformer (ViT) branch through a Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) gated fusion mechanism, allowing the model to combine fine-grained local texture cues with long-range global context in a single forward pass. The framework further incorporates a U-Net-based segmentation head to delineate tumor boundaries, a five-method Explainable AI (XAI) suite for transparent decision support, and a Large Language Model (LLM) module that converts model outputs into structured, human-readable clinical reports. Evaluated on the BRISC 2025 benchmark, which contains expert-annotated MRI scans spanning glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and healthy classes, the proposed model achieves 96.2% test accuracy while using only 7.8 million parameters, indicating that competitive diagnostic accuracy can be obtained without the computational burden typical of large-scale transformer or ensemble models. The results suggest that NeuroFusionNet is a practical candidate for deployment in resource-constrained clinical settings that still require interpretable, end-to-end decision support.

items.title: AI-Based Mobile Phone Screen Defect Detection Using OpenCV, YOLO, and Convolutional Neural Networks
items.abstract: Mobile phone screens are essential components of modern smartphones and may develop defects such as cracks,scratches, dark spots, and surface damage. Manual inspection can be time-consuming and may produce inconsistent results under changing lighting conditions. This paper presents a proposed artificial intelligence-based framework for automated mobile phone screen defect detection using OpenCV, You Only Look Once (YOLO), and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). OpenCV supports image acquisition and preprocessing, while YOLO is used to detect potential defects and estimate their locations. A CNN-based classifier may be incorporated when separate classification of detected regions is required. The system is designed to report defect categories, bounding boxes, and confidence scores, as well as indicate when no defect is detected above a selected threshold. The proposed framework describes the processing pipeline, system architecture, and evaluation strategy. Its effectiveness must be established through implementation and testing on a representative, accurately annotated dataset. Index Terms—Mobile phone screen, defect detection, OpenCV, YOLO, convolutional neural network, deep learning, computer vision, automated visual inspection.

items.title: AI-Based Risk Management and Crisis Response in Tourism Operations
items.abstract: Tourism is one of the most crisis-exposed industries in the modern economy. Natural disasters, terror attacks, political instability, cyber incidents, and pandemics repeatedly disrupt destinations and destination-serving firms, with cascading effects on workers, travellers, and host communities. Artificial intelligence now offers tourism operators a new generation of tools for anticipating, detecting, and responding to such disruptions, yet the adoption of these tools is as much an organisational and behavioural challenge as a technical one. This chapter analyses AI-based risk management and crisis response in tourism operations through an organisational behaviour lens. It integrates classical work on sensemaking, high-reliability organising, crisis management, and organisational resilience with tourism-specific research on crisis and disaster management and with emerging work on AI in hospitality and tourism.

items.title: AI-Driven Corporate Decision-Making and Directors' Fiduciary Duties: Can an Algorithm Replace the Boardroom?
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to analyse corporate data, forecast commercial outcomes, identify compliance risks and rank strategic alternatives. These capabilities can improve the speed and breadth of board-level analysis, but they also raise a fundamental question of company law: when an algorithm materially influences a corporate decision, who remains accountable for the outcome? This paper examines that question principally through section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013, which requires directors to act in good faith, exercise care, skill and diligence, and apply independent judgment. It argues that AI may support directors but cannot displace their fiduciary role. The central distinction is between using a system as an analytical aid and allowing its output to become a substitute for genuine deliberation. The paper considers automation bias, limited explainability, data quality, vendor dependence and the risk of fragmented accountability. It then draws carefully bounded lessons from the European Union’s AI regulatory framework and Indian financial regulation, before proposing governance measures concerning material-use disclosure, board competence, meaningful explanations, documentation, validation and continuing human responsibility. The paper concludes that corporate governance can become increasingly algorithm-assisted, but the legal responsibility for corporate judgment must remain traceable to accountable human decision-makers.

items.abstract: Advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and health care analytics has provided novel ways to personalize healthcare and implement precision medicine. This study suggests developing an AI-based personalized healthcare system based on analysis of patients' demographic details, health care history, lab results, genomic information, and current health parameters to predict their disease risks and make personalized treatment decisions. For implementation of this concept, machine learning models such as Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine, and neural network will be applied to analyze various data related to health care and identify patterns related to disease development and its treatment. Predictive analysis will be performed to determine patients' risk scores, probability of disease and treatment outcomes. Moreover, the use of explainable AI will enhance the transparency of predictions made. The proposed system will aim at 90-95% accuracy of predictions, about 30-40% decrease in time required to make diagnostics decisions and about 25-35% better early-risk detection than traditional approaches.

items.abstract: The rapid growth of scientific data from sensors, simulations, genomic research, high-performance computing, and collaborative research platforms has transformed the requirements of modern research data management (RDM). Traditional manual methods for organising, curating, and retrieving data are no longer sufficient to manage the scale and complexity of today's scientific ecosystems. This chapter explores how artificial intelligence technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, knowledge graphs, large language models, federated learning, and explainable AI are reshaping RDM into intelligent and adaptive infrastructures. It examines AI-enabled capabilities including automated data acquisition, semantic enrichment, predictive analytics, workflow automation, and responsible governance. The chapter also highlights applications across genomics, climate science, medicine, physics, social sciences, and materials science while discussing key technical, ethical, and organisational challenges.

items.abstract: The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Natural Language Processing (NLP) has expanded the use of automated techniques for resume analysis, recruitment matching, job recommendation, skill development, and interview preparation.This paper presents a comprehensive review of existing research on AIdriven resume analysis and placement support across five interconnected research areas: resume intelligence; semantic matching and Applicant Tracking System (ATS) evaluation; career and skill development; Large Language Model (LLM) and conversational support; and interview intelligence.The reviewed studies employ traditional NLP and machinelearning techniques such as regular expressions (regex), keyword matching, Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), Bag-of-Words (BoW), Word to Vector (Word2Vec), cosine similarity, k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Logistic Regression and fuzzy logic, together with Named Entity Recognition (NER), Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach (RoBERTa), distilled Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (DistilBERT), attention-based neural networks, collaborative filtering, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and LLM-based architectures.The literature shows a methodological progression from lexical and rule-based processing toward contextual, semantic, and generative approaches, with several studies reporting strong task-specific performance.At the same time, the evidence remains functionally fragmented: resume parsing and matching are extensively studied, while ATS evaluation, skill-gap analysis, learning support, conversational assistance, and AI-based interview preparation are addressed by smaller and more specialized groups of studies.The review identifies an integration gap in the literature, together with limitations related to dataset diversity, evaluation comparability, changing job requirements, explainability, fairness, privacy, and real-world validation.The findings provide a consolidated view of current methods, reported outcomes, and research opportunities in AI-supported resume analysis and placement preparation.

items.title: AI-Empowered Value Co-Creation for Intangible Cultural Heritage Digital Revitalization: A Conceptual Multi-Case Analysis
items.abstract: The digital revitalization of intangible cultural heritage (ICH) is central to China’s national strategy for digital culture. Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how ICH is safeguarded, transmitted, and innovated. Yet most studies focus on technological applications and have not systematically theorized how AI enters ICH value co-creation. Drawing on value co-creation theory, this study develops an analytical framework. It applies the framework through a conceptual multi-case analysis of eight publicly accessible online cases spanning different ICH domains and lead actors. Cross-case comparison tests the framework’s explanatory power. The findings identify four dominant models of ICH value co-creation under AI: heritage-bearer-led human-machine co-creation, public-platform-based crowd co-creation and benefit sharing, business-driven value monetization, and government-led ecosystem synergy. items.title: AI-enabled drug repurposing in Alzheimer’s disease: from computational nomination to pharmacological proof
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded the scale and speed of drug repurposing in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Transcriptomic signature matching, network-based systems pharmacology, real-world data pharmacoepidemiology and multi-omics machine learning have generated hundreds of candidate drugs, while repurposed agents account for 35% (56 of 158) of drugs and 42% (15 of 36) of Phase 3 agents in the 2026 AD pipeline. Clinical translation, however, remains unproven. Randomised trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists illustrate the gap between prioritisation and therapeutic proof: semaglutide did not slow clinical progression in evoke and evoke+, while liraglutide did not improve the primary FDG-PET endpoint in ELAD. We examine four complementary evidence domains, defining what each can and cannot establish, and position large language models as a cross-cutting tool for evidence synthesis and knowledge-graph reasoning rather than an independent source of biological evidence. Rather than cataloguing methods and candidates, we appraise leading drugs at the individual-molecule level and propose explicit criteria for progression from computational nomination to clinical testing. The framework defines seven requirements for clinical progression: disease-stage matching, adequate site-of-action exposure, including CNS exposure for central mechanisms, mechanistic validation in human-relevant models, biomarker-stratified trial design, convergence across independent evidence domains, causal inference with explicit boundary conditions, and mechanism-aligned endpoints with predefined stopping rules. AI has improved candidate prioritisation in AD, but clinical value will depend on converting ranked hypotheses into pharmacologically plausible and prospectively testable programmes.

items.abstract: This research paper, titled “AI-Powered Business Intelligence and Decision Making: A Literature Review and Conceptual Framework,” explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Business Intelligence (BI) to support effective, data-driven business decision-making. The paper reviews existing literature on machine learning, predictive analytics, explainable AI, and decision support systems. It proposes an eight-stage conceptual framework covering business problem identification, data collection, data validation, data integration, analytics, explanation of results, human decision-making, and continuous monitoring. The study also highlights challenges related to data quality, privacy, security, algorithmic bias, transparency, and model maintenance. A retail inventory example illustrates how AI-based forecasting can support managers in making informed decisions. This work is a literature review and conceptual study. The proposed framework has not yet been implemented or experimentally validated. Future work may involve developing a prototype and evaluating its effectiveness in a real-world business environment.

items.title: AI-Powered Swagger/OpenAPI Developer Assistant
items.abstract: Application Programming Interface (API) specifications written in the Swagger/OpenAPI format are the primary reference for developers who consume RESTful services, yet large specifications are time-consuming to read, cannot be queried in natural language, and must be tested and documented using separate tools. This paper presents the AI-Powered Swagger/OpenAPI Developer Assistant, a web-based platform that unifies these activities in a single workspace. A developer uploads a specification in JSON or YAML format; a Spring Boot back end parses it into structured endpoint information and supplies it as context to the Google Gemini large language model, which answers natural-language questions about endpoints, authentication, parameters, request and response schemas and error codes. The platform further provides an interactive API playground that builds request forms from the specification, executes live requests through a server-side executor and explains the returned response, together with a documentation generator for single endpoints or the complete API. The user interface is implemented in React with TypeScript. The paper describes the architecture, design decisions, implementation and security considerations of the system and discusses its advantages and limitations compared with a conventional multi-tool workflow.

items.title: AIoT Fault Diagnosis Maintenance Frameworks Based Metaheuristic and Two‐Stage Deep Learning Algorithms for Diesel Generators
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The reliable operation of diesel generators, which are critical devices in many industrial applications in maintaining continuous power supply, is essential. Objective This research presents an advanced Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) fault diagnosis framework that combines metaheuristic optimization and two‐stage deep learning methods to improve the fault classification accuracy of diesel generators. Methods The improved particle swarm optimization (IPSO) is used to fine‐tune the hyperparameters of bidirectional long short‐term memories (BiLSTM) combined with convolutional neural networks (CNN). The developed hybrid model aims to exploit the power of both the sequential learning of BiLSTMs and the feature extraction capability of CNNs to achieve superior fault diagnosis performance. Seven established baselines provide the point of reference for the IPSO‐BiLSTM‐CNN framework: recurrent neural network (RNN), CNN, gated recurrent unit (GRU), LSTM, bidirectional RNN (BiRNN), BiLSTM and CNN‐BiLSTM. Results Experimental results demonstrate that IPSO‐BiLSTM‐CNN methods outperform existing models in terms of accuracy and stability, achieving relative reductions of 71.56% in loss, 73.79% validating loss, 64.63% mean absolute error (MAE), 69.75% validating MAE, 23.17% cosine proximity (CP), 21.99% validating CP, 63.08% mean squared error (MSE), 71.55% validating MSE, together with relative improvements of 4.79% precision (PRE), 3.79% validating PRE, 5.8% recall (REC), and 5.29% validating REC. Conclusions This highlights its potential in practical AIoT applications for diesel generator monitoring and maintenance.

items.title: Algorithmic Constitutionalism in Mexico: Artificial Intelligence, Public Power, and the Transformation of Fundamental Rights
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing the scope of state action in the area of basic rights.AI use by public institutions is reshaping the scope of state action in the area of basic rights. This research aimed thus to evaluate the sufficiency of the Mexican constitution to control the use of AI by public bodies and to propose a model of algorithmic constitutionalism. A qualitative and documentary study was carried out in the field of algorithmic governance, reviewing constitutional norms, Mexican jurisprudence, academic studies and international instruments on issues such as transparency and explainability, human oversight and the protection of rights. The outcome shows that there are some bases for the regulation of automated decision making that are provided in the Mexican Constitution, specifically in the sections related to equality, data protection, access to information, due process and effective judicial protection. The regulatory landscape is divided and does not include a classification of risks, impact assessment, auditing or procedures to challenge algorithm decisions. Therefore, a democratic algorithmic constitutionalism model is presented, which is based on legal authorization, proportionality, transparency, explainability, human control, non-discrimination, judicial control, and accountability.

items.title: Algorithmic Postmodernism: A Framework
items.abstract: Algorithmic Postmodernism is a conceptual framework originated by Hoang-Dan Pham, conceived in 2024 with the founding of Hand-Fetish-Projects and formally stated in 2026. It describes a condition in which visibility increasingly precedes interpretation: search engines, recommendation systems and artificial-intelligence-based indexing decide what reaches attention before any person has encountered it, and so shape the conditions under which cultural value is recognised. It also takes a position: human beings should retain the power to decide what matters. Algorithmic Postmodernism is not a claim of total system control, and it takes no stance for or against artificial intelligence. Its specific contribution is to name a judge that evaluates each work from its own context, not from the context in which the work was made: a function with an authored goal and no authored rule. It locates that judge in art, the field built entirely on judging whether something deserves attention. The framework emerged from the practice of Hand-Fetish-Projects, an independent arthouse, and is positioned here against Lyotard, Baudrillard, Deleuze, Wiener and Doctorow.

items.title: Alpha: Systematic Fault Injection and Robustness Evaluation for LLM-Driven Embodied Manipulation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into embodied robotic planning, yet standard benchmarks primarily evaluate end-to-end task completion in nominal environments, obscuring failure origins across the execution stack. We present Alpha, a systematic fault-injection and robustness-evaluation framework for LLM-driven manipulation in simulation. Alpha injects calibrated faults across perception (sensor lag), actuation (grip slip), kinematics (unreachable targets), and planning (planner-output corruption), alongside concurrent conditions. To separate physical vulnerabilities from planner sensitivities, we introduce a matched methodology pairing an LLM agent (Llama-3 via Ollama) against a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner across a balanced 150-episode matrix under identical seeds, geometries, and safety criteria. Across the matrix, the Oracle achieves 64.0% (48/75) success while the LLM achieves 44.0% (33/75) (paired McNemar p = 3.01 x 10^-4). Crucially, excluding planner-output corruption, performance across all physical and kinematic conditions is identical: 55.0% (33/60) for both planners with zero discordant pairs (McNemar p = 1.00). This demonstrates that physical actuator slip, kinematic reach boundaries, and perceptual staleness affect deterministic controllers and LLM planners equivalently. The performance gap is driven entirely by planner-output corruption (100% Oracle vs. 0% LLM), isolating the prompt-to-JSON serialization and validation interface rather than a cognitive reasoning deficit. We also audit 169 historical pilot attempts for transparency.

items.title: An Adaptive Learning Framework for Educational Product Innovation
items.abstract: Digital learning increasingly combines platforms, artificial intelligence, multiple content formats, and social distribution, yet these elements are often designed as separate tools. This paper develops a conceptual framework for educational product innovation that connects these elements into an adaptive learning ecosystem. The study uses a conceptual synthesis approach. A focused synthesis of peer-reviewed literature and policy guidance on AI in education, adaptive learning, digital ecosystems, formative assessment, and social-media-supported learning was combined with a structured analysis of the framework and practical implementation examples documented in the author's 2026 monograph. The implementation examples are treated as illustrative cases rather than as an empirical evaluation. The resulting framework identifies three interacting infrastructure layers, digital products and platforms, artificial intelligence, and social distribution, and seven linked design processes: defining the learning need, packaging knowledge, building an owned digital home, augmenting with AI, designing the attention path, creating feedback loops, and measuring, learning and iterating. The framework integrates access, personalisation, engagement, assessment, and continuous improvement within one architecture. The framework offers a practical conceptual model for educators, learning designers, and education entrepreneurs developing technology-enabled learning experiences. It extends technology-centred approaches by treating distribution and feedback as integral parts of the learning ecosystem. Future research should empirically test the framework across educational settings and examine learner outcomes, equity, privacy, and sustainability.

items.title: An Explainable Hybrid AI–Gamification Framework for Adaptive E-Learning Systems with Simulation-Based Validation
items.abstract: Gamified e-learning platforms and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven adaptive learning systems can improve learner engagement, but existing solutions rarely combine the two, and few explain their adaptive decisions to learners. To address this gap, we propose LearnSpace, a hybrid AI–gamification framework for responsive e-learning that adds an Explanation Layer, based on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), to a deterministic reward architecture. The framework merges classical gamification mechanics with an AI personalization module in which experience points, rewards, and difficulty adjustments follow explicit weighted formulas. A Thompson-sampling bandit learns which feedback works best after a mistake. For each adaptive decision, the Explanation Layer names only the factors that drive it and turns them into a short justification for the learner. The design draws on a qualitative overview of 14 platforms, and the LearnSpace mobile prototype implements the gamification components and the bandit. In a pre-registered simulation with 500 synthetic learners per run, the first explanation rule named a factor that had no effect on the decision in 95.3% of difficulty adjustments, while the decision-specific rule never did. The bandit had lower regret than uniformly random feedback allocation. Effects on real learners remain to be tested.

items.title: An Explainable Zero-Trust Framework for Detecting Generative-AI-Enhanced Phishing and Credential Theft Using Real-World Threat Data
items.abstract: Phishing has evolved from simple fraudulent messages into a multi-channel credential-theft ecosystem thatcombines malicious URLs, QR-code phishing, adversary-in-the-middle proxying, business e-mail compromise,deepfake-assisted social engineering, and generative-AI-assisted content generation. This paper proposes anexplainable zero-trust framework for detecting and reducing phishing-related credential exposure using real-worldthreat intelligence and the PhiUSIIL public benchmark dataset. The study integrates APWG observations from2024 through Q3 2025 with a benchmark containing 235,795 URLs, 54 variables, 134,850 legitimate samples,and 100,945 phishing samples. The framework combines URL and page-content features, brand-mismatch evi-dence, QR-code detonation, sender-authentication signals, phishing-resistant MFA, conditional access, browserisolation, and human-readable explanations. A supervised benchmark experiment was conducted using a singlestratified 80/20 train-test split and three baseline classifiers. Decision Tree achieved 100.00% F1-score, RandomForest achieved 99.9975% F1-score, and Gaussian Naive Bayes achieved 98.1923% F1-score on the held-outtest set. These single-split benchmark results support a layered conclusion: URL detection is useful, but strongerrisk reduction is achieved when detection, identity, isolation, reporting, and continuous governance operate asone zero-trust system.

items.title: An Interactive Assistant to Support Security Operators
items.abstract: The security of Critical Infrastructures (CIs) is paramount, yet human operators frequently face cognitive overload when managing complex cyber-physical threats. This chapter presents a comprehensive overview of AVATAR4BC, a novel, personalized Intelligent Virtual Assistant (IVA) designed to address this critical human-factors challenge. Our system represents a paradigm shift from traditional dashboards by providing an embodied, conversational interface that leverages a high-fidelity 3D human avatar. A core contribution of AVATAR4BC is its multidisciplinary approach, which goes beyond technical integration. It fuses advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) with insights from the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH). The system’s backend integrates Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), and real-time speech-driven facial animation to create a natural interaction. Crucially, it incorporates Explainable AI (XAI) principles by using Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate human-readable explanations of opaque Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agent decisions from the underlying DYNABIC framework. Furthermore, AVATAR4BC’s personalization engine, informed by psychological and behavioral research, dynamically adapts the avatar’s appearance, voice, and communication style to the operator, aiming to reduce stress and enhance decision-making effectiveness. Final validation through end-to-end unit testing demonstrates the system’s core functionality, confirming the seamless integration of its architectural components. This work establishes a robust foundation for future research into human–AI collaboration, with significant implications for enhancing resilience in cybersecurity and other high-stakes domains.

items.title: Application and Optimization of Multimodal Knowledge Management in Web-Based English Teaching
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of digital transformation, English teaching is constrained by over-reliance on single-modal resources and insufficient integration of web technologies and pedagogy, which hinder the development of learners' higher-order skills. Using mixed-methods research, this study constructs a cognition-centered multimodal knowledge management framework based on cognitive load theory. It develops a system for resource classification, scenario adaptation, and cognitive activation alongside a three-dimensional tagging mechanism and an augmented reality‒supported technology-teaching double-helix model. Proper visual‒auditory input matching facilitates learners' information retention. Empirical evaluation reveals positive changes in classroom group interaction, digital tool adoption, and students' written logical performance. This study offers practical optimization strategies and suggests bridging the digital divide, strengthening teachers' technological pedagogical content knowledge capability, and exploring artificial intelligence applications for web-based multimodal English teaching.

items.title: APPLICATION OF DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES IN THE USE OF SOLAR ENERGY
items.abstract: This article analyzes the possibilities of applying modern digital technologies in solar energy systems. It examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), the Internet of Things (IoT), Digital Twin, Edge AI, cloud computing, Big Data, blockchain, drones, robotic maintenance, GIS, SCADA, smart inverters, and AR/VR technologies to improve the efficiency of solar photovoltaic power plants, forecast electricity generation, detect technical faults at an early stage, and optimize energy flow management. Digital technologies make it possible to monitor the real-time status of solar energy facilities, forecast power generation based on meteorological data, detect faults in panels and inverters, and automate maintenance. The article also highlights promising directions, including AI-based Digital Twins, Edge AI, federated learning, autonomous drone inspection, and blockchain-based peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading.
